Great questions — summarized answers below at a high level. I'll let Sean jump in with the technical specifics on PrivateLink/peering and IP behavior.

1) Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (high level):
- Hosted API: fastest to integrate, managed endpoints on Redwood infra. Good for low compliance requirements; not suitable if you require all traffic to remain in your VPC.
- Dedicated capacity: reserved GPU pools we run for you; lower latency variability and stronger data isolation but still egresses through Redwood-managed network unless configured with Private connectivity.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): best for regulated workloads requiring customer VPC control and network isolation. Supports PrivateLink or peering options depending on cloud provider.

Short recommendation: Given you said regulated payments and desire no public egress, Private (via PrivateLink or peering) is the right path.

Sean, can you provide the detailed networking options and any configuration notes?

Thanks,
Marissa

Hi Sara / Mike / Marissa,

Thanks — happy to lay out the options and recommended approach. Below are the common patterns we support on AWS, with pros/cons and configuration notes.

Option A — AWS PrivateLink (recommended for minimal customer-side network changes)
- Overview: We expose a service behind an NLB in our account; you create Interface VPC Endpoints (ENIs) in your VPC that connect to that service privately.
- Network footprint: traffic stays within the AWS backbone; no public IPs for data plane.
- Who configures what: Customer creates the Interface Endpoint(s) in their VPC and approves the endpoint connection. Redwood provides the service name and NLB config.
- CIDR/limits: Works across accounts; no overlapping CIDR requirement because traffic goes via endpoint ENIs.
- IP allowlisting: Because endpoints create ENIs in your VPC, inbound is from those ENIs; for egress-level allowlists (e.g., for outbound callbacks) we can provide a small set of egress IPs or support NAT through your own egress.

Option B — VPC Peering / Transit Gateway
- Overview: Direct peering between your VPC and Redwood's VPC (or through a Transit GW).
- Pros: Low latency and simpler routing for some architectures.
- Cons: Requires non-overlapping CIDRs; peering config is bi-directional and can be more operational overhead.
- Who configures what: Typically customer initiates peering request; Redwood accepts. For Transit GW, additional setup is required.

IP Allowlists and Egress
- Static egress IPs: If you require static egress IPs for firewall rules, we offer two approaches: (1) our managed NAT pool (small set of stable egress addresses) that we can reserve for your account, or (2) route egress through your NAT Gateway so IPs are under your control. We prefer the latter for strict audit requirements.

Certificates & KMS
- Certs: We can support customer-provided certificates. On AWS, you can use ACM with customer certs; Redwood will accept TLS from the PrivateLink/NLB front-end using your cert if desired.
- KMS: Redwood Private supports integration with customer KMS for data-at-rest encryption (customer-managed key) in Private deployments. We'll need IAM role details to allow cryptographic operations.

Attachments: I've uploaded a slightly more detailed sample network_diagram.png and our setup checklist (redwood-vpc-setup-guide.pdf) which outline required security groups, endpoint names, and port requirements (HTTPS on 443, optional metrics port 9090 for internal ops).

Next steps I suggest:
- Please share your VPC CIDR(s), a list of account IDs (if cross-account), and any constraints (no peering with X account, restricted AZs, etc.).
- Propose a 30-min call — we can draft a configuration during the call and agree on a small maintenance window for initial traffic routing.

Example: If you want fully customer-controlled egress and certs, best path is PrivateLink for inbound + route egress through your NAT Gateway. If you need very low-latency cross-account routing and no overlapping CIDRs, peering/transit is viable.

Let me know available times; happy to hop on.

Cheers,
